questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in past perfect tense form.

He dreamed of leaving his law firm to open a potable dog wash.
options: He was dreaming of leaving his law firm to open a portable dog wash.
He had dreamed of leaving his law firm to open a portable dog wash.
He had been dreaming of leaving his law firm to open a portable dog wash.
He has dreamed of leaving his law firm to open a portable dog wash.
questions.solution:
The formula which can structure a sentence into past perfect tense is:

Subject + had + past participle (third form of verb) + the rest of the sentence.

Among the given options, only option (b) matches the required formula. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:

Subject + will/shall + base form of verb (first form of verb) + the rest of the sentence.

Among the given options, only option (c) matches the required formula. Hence, (c) is the correct answer.

Therefore, the verb 'continued' is changed into 'had continued'.

Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in future continuous tense.

I will have sent the documents tomorrow afternoon.
options: I will send the documents tomorrow afternoon.
I will be sending the documents tomorrow afternoon.
I will have been sending the documents tomorrow afternoon.
I would send the documents tomorrow afternoon.
questions.solution:
The correct option that expresses the given sentence in the future continuous tense is option (b).

The future continuous tense is used to describe an action that will be ongoing at some point in the future. It is formed by using the future tense of the auxiliary verb, the verb "be", and the -ing form of the main verb.

Subject: "I" (pronoun indicating the person who will perform the action)

Future auxiliary verb: "will"

Present participle (be + base verb + -ing): "be sending"

Object: "the documents tomorrow afternoon" (what is being sent and when)

questions.question:

Shreya's sister has been sending him voice mails all morning.
Shreya's sister must be sending him voice mails all morning.
questions.solution:
The correct option that expresses the given sentence in the past perfect continuous tense is option (b).

The past perfect continuous tense is used to describe an action that was ongoing in the past and was happening continuously up to another point in the past. It is formed by using the past perfect tense of the auxiliary verb, the verb "been," and the -ing form of the main verb.

Subject: "Shreya's sister" (the person who performed the action)

Past perfect auxiliary verb: "had"

Past participle (been + base verb + -ing): "been sending"

Object: "him voice mails all morning" (what was being sent and when)

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in future tense form.

options: There were many exciting activities planned for the festival.
There will be many exciting activities planned for the festival.
There have been many exciting activities planned for the festival.
There had been many exciting activities planned for the festival.
questions.solution: The option that expresses the given sentence in future tense form is (b) (There will be many exciting activities planned for the festival). This option suggests that there are plans to organize numerous exciting activities for the festival that is yet to come. Option (a) is in the past tense, indicating that the activities were planned in the past. Option (c) is in the present perfect tense, suggesting that the activities have been planned up to the present time. Option (d) is in the past perfect tense, indicating that the activities were planned before a specific past time. Hence, (b) is the correct answer.

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in present perfect tense.

A) I had visited Paris several times in the past.

B) I visited Paris several times in the past.

C) I was visiting Paris several times in the past.

D) I have visited Paris several times in the past.
options: C
B
A
D
questions.solution:
The option that expresses the given sentence in present perfect tense is (d). The present perfect tense is used to indicate an action that was completed at an unspecified time in the past with a connection to the present. It is formed by using the following construct - "has/have + the past participle form (V3) of the main verb" (have visited). Only sentence D follows the correct structure of the present perfect tense. Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

Note:

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in the past tense form.

He will study diligently for the final History exam.
options: He studies diligently for the final History exam.
He is studying diligently for the final History exam.
He will be studying diligently for the final History exam.
He had studied diligently for the final History exam.
questions.solution:
The verb "will study" is in the future tense. To change it to the past tense, we need to consider the appropriate past tense form. Option (d) correctly changes the future tense "will study" to the past perfect tense "had studied." The past perfect tense is formed by using "had" + the past participle of the verb. In this case, the past participle of "study" is "studied." Hence, (d) is the correct answer.

Note: Participle: A word formed from a verb (e.g. going, gone, being, been) and used as an adjective (e.g. working woman, burnt toast) or a noun (e.g. good breeding). In English, participles are also used to make compound verb forms (e.g. is going, has been). Consider the sentences given below:

Dancing at the party, the women fell on the ground.

Encouraged by her parents, Rita went on to pursue her passion.

The highlighted word in the first sentence is of the form Verb + ing and is used as a present participle. It is used to denote an action that is going on or incomplete or imperfect.

The highlighted word in the second sentence is of the form verb + ed. It is used as a past participle. It denotes the completed action or state of the thing spoken of.

A past participle ends with the following: -ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n.

One should take great care and never get confused between a gerund and a present participle. They use the same forms but perform different functions: a gerund is a verbal noun, while a present participle is a verbal adjective.
